summary_en: Zuckerberg San Francisco General is the city's trauma centre and its safety-net hospital, and a great deal of public money is traceable to it by name: $237.9 million paid to vendors on contracts that name the hospital, alongside $130.9 million of voter-bond money expended on Building 5. The contracts show what running a hospital costs beside the rebuilding — $32.3 million paid to Clark Construction for chillers and cooling towers, $11.2 million for security guards, $4.1 million for hospital beds, $2.6 million to rent a chiller, $1.9 million for laboratory testing, $2.7 million for office supplies. The documents put that spending in context. A Controller's performance and efficiency review found the hospital at or near the top of a benchmark range for clinical quality in heart attacks, heart failure, pneumonia and the prevention of surgical infection, judged it productive and financially well run against comparable hospitals, and recorded an occupancy rate of 97 percent. A 1994 study of programmes affecting homeless people costed its treatment of patients who gave no address and had no third-party payer at $9,111,149 in a single year, most of it state money. And its institutional master plans track what it kept asking for: a medical helipad, which the Health Commission requested a feasibility study for after the 2001 trauma care plan exposed the city's geographic isolation; new emergency generator capacity; and a new acute care hospital.

The Trauma Care System Plan revealed vulnerabili- ties in San Francisco's ability to prevent death and disability due to injury. The trauma system vulnerabilities - geographic isolation, traffic congestion, population density - are especially aggrevated by the lack of air medical

tained by young children, requiring immediate transfer to Oakland Children's Pediatric Trauma Center In September 2002, the San Francisco Health Commission approved an agreement with the San Francisco architectural firm of Gerson/Overstreet to provide analytical, planning and architectural services for the San Francisco General Hospital Air Medical Access Needs and Feasibility Study. The final work products of the contract are: (1) a written report to the San Francisco Health Commission and Executive Administrator of San Francisco General Hospital documenting the study findings, and (2) a presentation to a regularly scheduled meeting of the San Francisco Health Commission. There were two parts to the study effort.
